title: Voltra E-Bikes: warranty provision, expected refunds, adjusting entries and disclosure ethics
participant_role: Staff accountant at Voltra E-Bikes preparing the first year-end adjusting entries
judge_role: Founder of Voltra E-Bikes, who wants to delay recording warranty costs and returns to keep profits high for an investor pitch

difficulty.rationale: The auditors' guidance explains how to handle warranties and expected refunds, so students apply the method to the numbers instead of recalling revenue recognition rules.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a staff accountant at VOLTRA E-BIKES, a company that designs and sells electric bicycles. The founder (judge) has asked you to review your year-end adjusting entries before the financial statements are shared with investors.

VOLTRA E-BIKES has just finished its first year of business. The company sold 400 e-bikes this year at $1,500 each, for revenue of $600,000. Each bike cost $900. Every bike comes with a 2-year repair warranty. Industry data shows that 6% of bikes will need a warranty repair, at an average cost of $250 per repair. During this year, 10 bikes were repaired under warranty at $250 each, and the $2,500 was paid in cash.

The company also offers a 30-day money-back guarantee. Sixty bikes were sold in December, so their return period is still open at year end. Historically, 5% of bikes are returned for a full refund. Returned bikes can be resold and are recorded at cost.

Guidance from the company's auditors: estimate warranty cost in the year of sale using historical rates; for the 30-day money-back guarantee, reduce sales and record a refund liability for expected refunds, and record the cost of bikes expected to be returned as an asset (Estimated Inventory Returns) that reduces cost of goods sold.

The founder (judge) is preparing an investor pitch next month and wants to "keep profits high." The founder (judge) plans to record warranty costs only when repairs actually happen and to ignore returns until customers bring bikes back.

[Voltra E-Bikes first-year data: see exhibits]

You must:
- Explain what a provision is and why GAAP requires estimating it
- Compute the warranty expense and the year-end warranty liability
- Apply the auditors' guidance to record the adjusting entries for warranties and expected refunds
- Show the impact on net income compared with the founder's plan
- Explain the disclosure requirements and the ethics issue

You will present the information to the founder (judge) in a role-play to take place in the founder's (judge's) office. The founder (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the founder's (judge's) questions, the founder (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: What if actual repairs next year cost more than $3,500?
Our investors are sophisticated. Won't they figure out the numbers anyway?

solution.overview: A strong answer explains that GAAP requires estimating warranty and refund costs in the year of the sale (matching and expense recognition), computes $6,000 of warranty expense with a $3,500 year-end liability and a $4,500 refund liability offset by a $2,700 returns asset, and records four entries. The presenter shows that GAAP income is $5,300 lower and liabilities $8,000 higher than under the founder's plan, then explains the required note disclosures and why understating liabilities misleads investors.

by_task.task: What a provision is and why GAAP requires it
answer: A provision is a liability of uncertain timing or amount, estimated and recorded now
The warranty promise and the refund right were created when the bikes were sold this year
Matching (expense recognition): the costs belong in the same period as the $600,000 of revenue
Recording costs only when paid would overstate this year's profit and understate liabilities
Expected repairs: 400 x 6% = 24 bikes
Warranty expense: 24 x $250 = $6,000
Repairs already paid this year: $2,500
Year-end Estimated Warranty Liability: 6,000 minus 2,500 = $3,500
(a) Accrue warranty expense of $6,000
(b) Record the $2,500 of repairs paid as a reduction of the liability, not a new expense
(c) Expected returns: 60 x 5% = 3 bikes; record a $4,500 refund liability through Sales Returns and Allowances
(d) Record the 3 bikes expected back as a $2,700 Estimated Inventory Returns asset, reducing cost of goods sold
GAAP expense effect: 6,000 warranty + (4,500 minus 2,700 = 1,800) net returns = $7,800
Founder's plan expenses only the $2,500 of repairs paid
GAAP net income is 7,800 minus 2,500 = $5,300 lower this year
Liabilities are $8,000 higher: 3,500 warranty + 4,500 refunds
Notes must describe the warranty terms and reconcile the liability: beginning 0, accrued 6,000, settled 2,500, ending 3,500
Disclose the refund policy and the estimates used
Investors rely on these notes to judge future cash outflows
Knowingly leaving out these liabilities to inflate profit is fraudulent financial reporting
An accountant's duty is to present fairly, even when the boss wants a better number

journal_entries.description: (a) Accrue estimated warranty cost on this year's sales
(b) Warranty repairs paid during the year
(c) Expected refunds on December sales (3 bikes x $1,500)
(d) Expected return of 3 bikes to inventory at cost (3 x $900)

calculations.label: Warranty expense and year-end liability
steps: 6,000 minus 2,500 paid = $3,500 liability at year end

judge_question_answers.question: What if actual repairs next year cost more than $3,500?
answer: That is a change in accounting estimate, which is normal and not an error
Record the extra cost in the period we learn about it (prospectively); do not restate this year
Review the 6% rate and $250 average cost every period using our own repair history
A good-faith estimate is required even though it will not be exact

judge_question_answers.question: Our investors are sophisticated. Won't they figure out the numbers anyway?
answer: Investors rely on GAAP statements and notes; they cannot see our internal repair data
If they find understated liabilities later, we lose credibility and possibly the investment
Deliberately misleading investors can be fraud with legal consequences
Honest, well-explained estimates show strong management and build trust

key_concepts.definition: A liability whose amount or timing is uncertain, such as warranties or customer refunds, that is estimated and recorded when the obligation arises.
Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenues they help earn, so warranty costs for this year's sales are expensed this year.
The estimated cost of future repairs on products already sold. Warranty expense = units sold x expected repair rate x average cost per repair.
The balance of warranty costs expected but not yet paid. Ending liability = beginning + expense accrued minus repairs paid.
The amount the company expects to refund to customers who return goods. Refund liability = expected returns x selling price.
An asset for goods expected to come back from customers, recorded at cost because they can be resold. It reduces cost of goods sold.
A contra revenue account that reduces sales for goods returned or expected to be returned.
An entry made at the end of the period so revenues, expenses, assets and liabilities are reported in the correct period.
An update to an estimate when new information appears. It is recorded in the current and future periods, not by restating past statements.
Explanations that accompany the statements, such as warranty terms and a reconciliation of the warranty liability, so users understand the numbers.
Intentionally misstating or leaving out amounts or disclosures to mislead users, such as understating liabilities to make profits look higher.

notes: State level because students must build four adjusting entries, including the refund liability and inventory returns asset described in the auditors' guidance, and then quantify the income effect against the founder's plan. Watch for students who expense the $2,500 of repairs on top of the $6,000 accrual (double counting), who record the full $4,500 refund with no inventory asset, or who treat the estimate as optional because it is uncertain.

criteria.exceeds: Defines a provision as a liability of uncertain timing or amount, explains that the warranty and refund obligations were created when the bikes were sold this year so matching requires the cost now, and calculates 24 expected repairs, $6,000 of warranty expense and a $3,500 year-end liability.
criteria.meets: Explains that GAAP requires estimating the warranty cost in the year of sale and calculates warranty expense of $6,000 (400 x 6% x $250) and a year-end liability of $3,500.
criteria.below: Knows an estimate is needed but gets the numbers partly wrong, for example reports a $6,000 liability without subtracting the $2,500 already paid.
criteria.little: Does not explain provisions, or agrees with the founder that warranty costs can wait until repairs happen.

criteria.exceeds: Records all four entries correctly (debit Warranty Expense $6,000, credit Estimated Warranty Liability $6,000; debit Estimated Warranty Liability $2,500, credit Cash $2,500; debit Sales Returns and Allowances $4,500, credit Refund Liability $4,500; debit Estimated Inventory Returns $2,700, credit Cost of Goods Sold $2,700) and explains how posting them leaves a $3,500 warranty balance.
criteria.meets: Records the warranty accrual of $6,000, the $2,500 repairs charged against the liability, and the $4,500 refund liability with the $2,700 inventory returns asset.
criteria.below: Records only some entries, expenses the $2,500 of repairs on top of the $6,000 accrual, or records the $4,500 refund with no inventory asset.
criteria.little: Gives no journal entries, or entries with unrelated accounts.

criteria.exceeds: Shows that GAAP expenses total $7,800 ($6,000 warranty + $1,800 net returns) versus $2,500 under the founder's plan, so net income is $5,300 lower and liabilities are $8,000 higher ($3,500 + $4,500), and explains why the founder's plan overstates this year's profit.
criteria.meets: Calculates expected returns of 3 bikes ($4,500 refund, $2,700 at cost, $1,800 net) and shows GAAP net income is $5,300 lower than the founder's plan.
criteria.below: Compares the two approaches with missing or wrong numbers, for example uses the full $4,500 as the income effect or skips the liability difference.
criteria.little: Does not compare GAAP with the founder's plan, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibit.

items.label: Explain financial disclosure regulations and policies

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the notes must describe the warranty terms and reconcile the liability (beginning $0, accrued $6,000, settled $2,500, ending $3,500), disclose the refund policy and estimates used, and that investors rely on these notes to judge future cash outflows.
criteria.meets: States that the notes must describe the warranty and refund policies, the estimates used, and the change in the warranty liability.
criteria.below: Mentions that disclosures are needed but cannot say what they should include.
criteria.little: Does not address disclosure, or suggests the estimates can be left out of the statements.

items.label: Discuss the role of ethics in accounting

criteria.exceeds: Explains that knowingly leaving out $8,000 of liabilities to show investors a higher profit is fraudulent financial reporting, and that an accountant's duty is to present fairly even when the boss wants a better number, while offering to explain honest estimates in the pitch.
criteria.meets: Explains that ignoring the warranty and refund estimates to keep profits high would mislead investors and that the accountant must follow GAAP.
criteria.below: Says the founder's plan is not allowed but does not explain the ethical issue or who is harmed.
criteria.little: Does not address ethics, or goes along with the founder's plan.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the sales to the warranty and refund obligations, the four entries, the $5,300 income effect, the $8,000 liability effect and the note disclosures investors will read.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit data to the warranty and refund estimates and their effect on income.
criteria.below: Reaches conclusions without showing the reasoning, or double counts the $2,500 of repairs.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the founder a clear decision to record all four entries before the statements go to investors, and suggests presenting the estimates as a sign of strong management in the pitch.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation to follow the auditors' guidance and record the warranty and refund estimates.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or accepts the founder's plan.

criteria.exceeds: Explains provisions and matching in plain language the founder can follow, in a logical order from concept to numbers to entries to impact, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the calculations, entries, income comparison and disclosures clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses an effective visual such as a side by side comparison of GAAP and the founder's plan or a T-account of the warranty liability, and adds a useful idea such as tracking the company's own repair history to refine the 6% rate.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the estimates and their effect easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: repairs above $3,500 are a normal change in estimate recorded in the period learned (not a restatement), with the 6% rate and $250 cost reviewed each period; and investors cannot see internal repair data, so understated liabilities would cost credibility, could be fraud, and honest estimates build trust.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that extra repair costs are a change in estimate recorded going forward and that investors rely on the GAAP statements and notes.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without reasons.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says this year must be restated or that investors will not care.

key_points: A provision is a liability of uncertain timing or amount; matching requires recording warranty and refund costs in the year of sale
Warranty expense: 400 x 6% = 24 repairs x $250 = $6,000; year-end liability $6,000 minus $2,500 paid = $3,500
Expected returns: 60 x 5% = 3 bikes; Refund Liability $4,500 (3 x $1,500) and Estimated Inventory Returns $2,700 (3 x $900)

Entries: debit Warranty Expense, credit Estimated Warranty Liability $6,000; debit Estimated Warranty Liability, credit Cash $2,500; debit Sales Returns and Allowances, credit Refund Liability $4,500; debit Estimated Inventory Returns, credit Cost of Goods Sold $2,700
GAAP expenses $7,800 versus $2,500 under the founder's plan, so net income is $5,300 lower and liabilities are $8,000 higher
Notes must describe warranty terms and reconcile the liability ($0 + $6,000 minus $2,500 = $3,500) and disclose the refund policy and estimates
Leaving out these liabilities to inflate profit for investors is fraudulent financial reporting
